lead: The output layer turns the last hidden vector into a prediction, and the loss function scores that prediction against the target. The two are chosen as a pair, decided by the target: a real number needs a linear output with mean squared error, a yes/no answer needs a sigmoid with binary cross-entropy, and one of K classes needs a softmax with categorical cross-entropy. Get the pair wrong and training stalls or misbehaves. Every practical network ends this way, from a bank flagging a defaulting loan to a phone keyboard guessing the next word.
prereq: You need: 1.7 Activation functions for sigmoid and softmax, and 1.6 Multilayer perceptrons for what the vector h is.

blocks.text: A network's last layer is the output layer. It turns the final hidden vector h into a prediction ŷ or a probability p. The loss function then compares that prediction with the target y and returns one number: how wrong the model was on this single example. Training nudges the weights to make that number small.
Loss and output layer come as a pair, and the target decides the pair, not taste. A target can be only three things:

items: A real number, such as tomorrow's temperature in °C or a house price in rupees. Output: a linear unit. Loss: mean squared error.
One of two classes, such as "will this UPI payment fail?". Output: a sigmoid unit giving p in (0, 1). Loss: binary cross-entropy.
One of K classes, such as which of 10 digits is in an image. Output: softmax over K units. Loss: categorical cross-entropy.

blocks.text: The loss L is the penalty on one example. The cost J is the average of the loss over a batch of n examples; minimising the cost is the optimiser's job, covered in Unit 2.

blocks.where: J is the cost over the batch; n is the number of examples in the batch; Lᵢ is the loss on example i; Σᵢ adds over i = 1 to n.

blocks.text: Regression. The output unit is linear: ŷ = w·h + b, where w is the weight vector, h the hidden vector, b the bias, and ŷ a real number with no squashing. Over one example the squared error loss is L = (ŷ − y)². If y is in rupees, L is in rupees squared, so report √L to get back to rupees. Mean absolute error, L = |ŷ − y|, resists outliers, but its gradient is ±1 everywhere, so it never eases off near the answer.
Two classes. The output unit is a sigmoid, p = 1/(1 + e^(−z)) with z = w·h + b, so p is the model's probability that y = 1. The loss is binary cross-entropy:
L = −[y log p + (1 − y) log(1 − p)]
blocks.where: y is the target, exactly 0 or 1; p is the predicted probability of class 1, in (0, 1); log is the natural logarithm.

blocks.text: When y = 1 only −log p survives: it is 0 at p = 1 and grows without limit as p → 0, so a confident mistake is punished hard. When y = 0 only −log(1 − p) survives. A plain linear unit also handles two classes: train it with MSE and predict class 1 when ŷ > 0.5. It is simple, but the output is unbounded and is not a probability, and MSE keeps pulling on points that are already correctly classified far from the boundary (ŷ = 10 with y = 1 still has gradient 2(10 − 1)), so outliers dominate the fit. Cross-entropy is the usual choice.

sections.h3: K classes and the clean gradient

blocks.text: For K classes the output layer has K units, one per class, each with a logit z_k = w_k·h + b_k. Softmax turns the logit vector into probabilities:

blocks.where: z_k is the logit of class k; p_k is the predicted probability of class k; the sum in the denominator runs over all j = 1 to K. Every p_k is positive and the K values add to 1.

blocks.text: The target is now a class index. Write p_y for the probability the model gave to the correct class. The loss is categorical cross-entropy, L = −log p_y. A perfect prediction gives L = 0; giving the true class only 0.09 costs 2.41.

This pair is standard because of its gradient. With softmax followed by cross-entropy, ∂L/∂z_k = p_k − y_k, where y is the one-hot target (1 at the true class, 0 elsewhere). The softmax derivative cancels completely, so the gradient is as clean as ŷ − y for a linear unit. 1.9 shows how this flows back through the network.

Two coding habits. Clip p to a floor such as 1e−12 before the log, because log 0 is −∞ and one bad example can wreck a batch. In the softmax itself, subtract the largest logit from every z_k first: the ratios are unchanged and e^z cannot overflow.

figure.caption: The worked example: logits (2, 1, 0) become probabilities (0.665, 0.245, 0.090); the true class 3 costs 2.41 nats. The gradient at the logits is just p − y = (0.665, 0.245, −0.910).

spec.aria: Flowchart of the worked example: logits (2, 1, 0) are exponentiated and summed to 11.1074, divided to give softmax probabilities (0.665, 0.245, 0.090), the true class 3 gives loss 2.41, and the gradient at the logits is (0.665, 0.245, −0.910).

examples.question: A 3-class classifier has logits z = (2, 1, 0). (a) Find the softmax probabilities. (b) Find the loss if the true class is the third one, and the gradient at the logits. (c) Find the loss if the true class is the first one.
steps: True class 1: L = −log 0.665 = 0.41. Being right costs little; being wrong on this example costs 2.41.
examples.answer: Probabilities (0.665, 0.245, 0.090); loss 2.41 nats if the true class is the third, 0.41 if it is the first.
examples.check:
import math
z = [2.0, 1.0, 0.0]
e = [math.exp(v) for v in z]
s = sum(e)
p = [v / s for v in e]
print(round(p[0], 3))
print(round(p[1], 3))
print(round(p[2], 3))
print(round(-math.log(p[2]), 2))
print(round(-math.log(p[0]), 2))
g = [p[k] - (1 if k == 2 else 0) for k in range(3)]
print(round(g[2], 3))

traps: Using MSE with a sigmoid or softmax output for classification. The squash saturates exactly when the model is confidently wrong, so the gradient nearly vanishes while the error is largest. Use cross-entropy with a squashed output.
Taking the log of a probability that reached 0; log 0 is −∞, so one example poisons the batch average. Clip to 1e−12. Examiners also test L = −log p_y, not L = −log(1 − p_y).
Confusing loss with cost, or dropping the 1/n: a missing factor of n scales every gradient by n.
Applying softmax twice, once in the output layer and again on the already-normalised p in the loss.
For categorical cross-entropy, using −log p_y where p_y is the probability of the wrong class, or forgetting that only one term survives because the target is one-hot.

quiz.q: Which loss pairs with a softmax output layer, and what is its formula?
quiz.a: Categorical cross-entropy, L = −log p_y, where p_y is the probability the model gave to the true class.

quiz.q: Which output unit and which loss are used for regression, and what units does the loss carry?
quiz.a: A linear unit ŷ = w·h + b and squared error L = (ŷ − y)². If y is in rupees, L is in rupees squared, so √L is the error in rupees.

quiz.q: Why does sigmoid plus squared error learn slowly when the model is confidently wrong?
quiz.a: The sigmoid derivative σ(1 − σ) is near 0 at both ends. When the model outputs 0.99 for a true class 0, the error is large but the derivative is 0.0099, so the gradient reaching the weights is tiny. Cross-entropy cancels that derivative and gives a gradient of size p − y.

quiz.q: State the difference between a loss and a cost in one sentence each.
quiz.a: The loss L is the penalty on a single example. The cost J is the mean of the losses over a batch, J = (1/n) Σ Lᵢ, and it is what gradient descent minimises.

quiz.q: Logits are z = (1, 1) and the true class is the first one. Find the softmax probabilities, the loss, and the gradient at the logits.
A binary classifier outputs p = 0.2 and the target is y = 1. Find the binary cross-entropy.
quiz.a: y = 1 kills the second term, so L = −log 0.2 = 1.609.

quiz.q: A 3-class softmax gives p = (0.7, 0.2, 0.1) and the true class is the second. Find ∂L/∂z and explain why the entries must sum to 0.
quiz.a: ∂L/∂z_k = p_k − y_k with y = (0, 1, 0), so the gradient is (0.7, −0.8, 0.1). The sum is 0 because softmax output is constrained to add to 1: raising one probability forces the others down, so gradient steps only redistribute mass, never change the total.

quiz.q: A model outputs p = 0.999 for a sample whose true class is 1. Explain why the loss is small here but clipping still matters elsewhere.
quiz.a: L = −log 0.999 = 0.001, correctly small. But when a sample is confidently wrong, softmax can give the true class probability that underflows to 0 in floating point; log 0 is −∞ and the batch cost becomes not a number. Clipping to 1e−12 caps the loss near 27.6 and keeps training alive.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production systems keep the pairing but reshape one side of it: label smoothing softens the one-hot target to stop overconfidence, focal loss down-weights easy examples when one class dominates, and temperature scaling divides the logits before softmax to make predicted probabilities honest. Some models predict a whole distribution — the mean and variance of a Gaussian, trained with a likelihood loss. Useful search terms: focal loss, label smoothing, temperature scaling, heteroscedastic regression loss.
